newsitem.title: CHINA: China marks Shanghai Communique with stab at U.S..
newsitem.headline: China marks Shanghai Communique with stab at U.S..

text.p: China on Friday marked the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Communique, the starting point for the process of normalising Sino-U.S. relations, with a swipe at Washington for failing to honour the terms of its agreements.

The official People's Daily said in a commentary that the communique had provided a foundation for the healthy development of Sino-American ties, but that relations continued to suffer due to problems on the U.S. side.

It accused the United States of continually violating the terms of the Shanghai Communique and two subsequent joint declarations -- a communique in 1978 establishing diplomatic relations and a further one in 1982.
"Very often, due to the failure of the U.S. side to respect the principles laid down in the three communiques, relations between the two countries have fallen into difficulties," it said.
"Especially over the Taiwan question, the U.S. side constantly engenders words and actions which violate the communiques," it said.

Relations between China and the United States deteriorated markedly during 1996 due to a host of disputes ranging from Taiwan to pirated software and illegal garbage shipments, and have only improved somewhat in recent months.
A western diplomat said both sides seemed happy with this week's visit to Beijing by new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

The Shanghai Communique was signed in a local hotel on February 28, 1972, at the end of an historic visit to China by then U.S. president Richard Nixon which he described as "the week that changed the world".

After long wrangling, the two sides agreed to disagree in writing on a number of key issues, with Washington acknowledging that there was only one China without saying specifically what it was or where it had its capital.

Since losing their civil war with Mao Zedong's communists on the mainland in 1949, the Chinese Nationalists have made their base on the island of Taiwan and still claim to be the rightful government of all China.
"We need to continue to use the spirit of the Shanghai Communique in our relations," said Professor Zhao Dunren of the Fudan University American Centre.
"We must continue to seek out the points of agreement, and put to one side the points of disagreement until the time is ripe to handle them," he added.
A western analyst in Shanghai agreed. "The key to the communique was the ambiguity with which the two sides agreed to disagree."
"Its spirit allows Taiwan to continue its de facto separate existence with unification at some point under some regime in the future," he added.

Analysts said much of the Shanghai Communique's ambiguity was clarified in the 1978 communique on diplomatic relations, with the United States recognising Beijing as the capital of China and Taiwan as a province of China.

But Washington reserved the right to provide arms and military assistance to the Taipei government under another communique in 1982, which said only that arms sales would cease after a certain period of time.
"There is the question of how to define 'after a period of time'," said Ding Xinghao, president of the Chinese Association for American Studies.

China escalated pressure on Taiwan during the island's presidential election campaign last March, conducting a series of missile test firings into waters close to Taiwan's main ports. The United States responded by moving naval forces into the Taiwan Strait.

"The assumption on the U.S. side with the communiques has been that China will not use force to solve the Taiwan question," said the western analyst. "But if the equation changes, that could result in a change in the U.S. response."
